transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Yeah, thank you. Well, my wife actually pushed me to make the appointment, but... I guess I know she's right to be worried. What really brings me in is just... I don't feel real happiness anymore. Or closeness, or joy, or anything like that. It's like that whole part of me is just completely shut off. 

Take our weekends, for example. We used to have this whole Sunday routine, right? I'd wake up early, make the coffee, we'd sit out on the back patio for a couple of hours, maybe go for a drive later in the afternoon. It was our thing, just a really nice way to reset for the week. She still tries to get me to do it, you know? She sets everything up, makes the coffee exactly how I used to like it, tries to get me to just sit and enjoy the morning with her. And I sit there, and I look at her, and I know I love her, but I just feel... nothing. Just completely hollow. 

And it's not just at home, either. I'm a manager, I oversee a pretty sizable team, and last week we finally closed this massive account we've been chasing for the better part of six months. My boss was thrilled, the team was celebrating, ordering food, all of that. A while back, I would have been over the moon, feeling proud of the hard work, taking everyone out to celebrate. But when the email came through that we got it... I just went back to my office and stared at my desk. I couldn't even fake a smile for my team. It's just this constant, heavy blankness where the good stuff is supposed to be. I just can't connect to those feelings anymore, no matter how hard I try.
Have you noticed a decrease in your interest or enjoyment in activities that you used to find pleasurable, like your Sunday routine or work achievements?

Well, yeah, exactly. That's... that's exactly what I was just saying, I guess. I mean, the Sunday routine, the work stuff, it's all just gone. The interest is just completely gone. I used to love those mornings. I mean, I would actually look forward to them all week. I'd buy this specific roast from a local place downtown, just for Sundays, and I'd grind the beans fresh... the whole house would smell like it. And my wife and I would just talk about everything and nothing. It was this perfect little bubble. Now, she brings me a mug, and I just look at the steam rising off it, and it's just... a cup of hot liquid. There's no joy in it. I don't care about the coffee, I don't care about sitting on the patio. I just want to go back to bed, or just sit in a dark room where I don't have to pretend. 

And work... work is almost worse, because I'm supposed to be leading these people. I've been a manager for twelve years, and I've always prided myself on being the guy who rallies the troops, you know? When we get a big win, I'm the one popping the champagne, metaphorically speaking. But this last account... my god, the hours we put in. My lead analyst, Sarah, she practically lived at the office for two weeks straight to get the projections right. And when we finally got the green light, she came into my office, practically vibrating with excitement, and I just... I had nothing for her. I think I said, "Good job, log it in the system," and turned back to my monitor. I could see the wind just completely leave her sails. I felt terrible about it logically, but emotionally? I couldn't even muster up the energy to care that I was ruining her moment. It's like the part of my brain that registers accomplishment or satisfaction has just been scooped out. So, yeah, the enjoyment is definitely gone. Completely.
How long have you been feeling this way?

Well, it feels like an absolute lifetime, honestly, but if I really sit down and look at the calendar... it has been about a year and seven months. Yeah, exactly a year and seven months, actually. It all started right after the retrofit accident. Before that, everything was fine, you know? I was the guy making the Sunday coffee, rallying the team, doing all the normal things a person does. But then the accident happened during that major retrofit project we were overseeing at work. It was a massive undertaking, lots of moving parts, contractors everywhere, and then the accident just... it changed everything. 

And you would think, maybe after a few weeks or a couple of months, you would bounce back. You would get back to normal. My wife kept telling me to just give it time, that I was just processing things and I just needed to ride it out and be patient with myself. So I waited. I waited through the holidays that first year, thinking maybe Thanksgiving or the new year would snap me out of it, bring back some of that joy or at least a little bit of warmth when we had the family over to the house. But there was just nothing. Then spring came, then summer, and now here we are, a year and seven months down the line from the day of that retrofit accident, and it has just been this exact same heavy blankness every single day since. 

It hasn't lifted for a minute. Not even for a second. I keep looking back at who I was before that job, before that specific day, and it is like looking at a completely different person. I just don't understand how nineteen whole months can go by and I am still just stuck in this void, you know? It just drags on and on, and every month that passes where I still feel this empty just makes it harder to believe I will ever get back to being the guy who actually cared about things.
Have you felt this way — emotionally empty, without joy or interest in things — every day, without any significant break or improvement, since the accident?

Yeah. Every single day. I know I just sort of rambled about it, but... yes. It's been this exact same way since the retrofit accident. Like I said, about a year and seven months ago. And when I say every day, I really mean it. It's not like I have a good week and then a bad week, or even a good afternoon where I suddenly feel like myself again and then it fades. It's just... constant. 

I remember reading somewhere, or maybe someone told me—one of those well-meaning friends who tries to give you advice when you're clearly struggling—that grief or trauma or whatever this is, comes in waves. You know? They say you have a good day, and then a wave hits you, and you're down again, but eventually the waves get farther apart. But that's not what this is. There are no waves. It's just a flatline. Since that day on the site, since the accident... it's just been a year and seven months of absolute flatline. 

I wake up, and the emptiness is there before I even open my eyes. I go to work, and it sits there with me in every meeting, every email I send. I come home, and it sits between me and my wife at the dinner table. And there hasn't been a single break in it. Not a vacation, not a holiday, not a birthday. We even tried going away for our anniversary last fall, up to this cabin in the mountains we used to love. I thought maybe getting away from the city, away from the office, maybe the fresh air would do something. My wife planned the whole thing, packed all my favorite foods, booked a place with a fireplace. And I just sat in front of that fire for three days feeling absolutely nothing. The fire was warm, but I couldn't feel the comfort of it, if that makes sense. So, yes. Every day. Since the accident, a year and seven months ago, without fail.
Have you noticed that you feel a lack of energy or increased fatigue almost every day, even when you haven’t done anything physically or mentally exhausting?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I'm not physically exhausted in the way you're describing, like where my body just can't move or I need to sleep all day. It's not like that. Honestly, I'm still doing all the things I'm supposed to do, physically speaking. I get up, I shower, I put on my suit, I drive to the office, I sit through the meetings. My body works fine. I'm not dragging my feet or feeling like I ran a marathon when I just walked to the mailbox. 

It's more like... well, like I was saying before about the emptiness. It's not a lack of physical energy, it's a lack of *caring*. So I don't feel fatigued in my muscles, you know? I'm 47, I'm in decent shape, I don't have any physical health problems. But it's just that heavy blankness I mentioned. I can physically walk into the kitchen and make the coffee, but the *drive* to do it, the spark that makes you want to do anything at all... that's what's missing. 

I remember when I first started as a manager, I used to work 60-hour weeks, and I'd come home dead on my feet, completely physically wiped out. My bones would ache. But I still had energy, if that makes sense. I had mental energy. I'd sit on the couch with my wife and we'd talk for another two hours because I was so wired from the day. This isn't like that. This isn't fatigue. It's just... I'm physically capable, I just have absolutely no desire to use the capability. So, no, I wouldn't say I feel unusually tired or fatigued in that sense. Just hollowed out.
Have you found yourself feeling worthless or guilty about things almost every day, even when there's no clear reason for it?

No, not really. I mean, I don't feel guilty. Worthless? No, I wouldn't use that word either. It's... well, it goes back to what I was just saying, right? About that emptiness. To feel worthless or guilty, you have to actually feel something, don't you? You have to care enough about yourself or your actions to judge them. And I just don't. 

I mean, take my wife, for instance. She's been incredible through all of this, for the whole year and seven months since the retrofit accident. She picks up the slack, she plans things, she tries to keep the house running smoothly while I just exist in this void. And you'd think I'd feel guilty about that. A normal person would feel guilty that their spouse is carrying all the weight, right? I can intellectually recognize that I *should* feel guilty. I can look at her doing the dishes after working a full day herself and think, "I am not contributing the way a husband should." But the actual emotion of guilt? The pit in your stomach, the shame? It's just not there. 

It's the same with work. I'm the manager. I'm supposed to be leading the team. And I know I'm not doing it with the same vigor I used to. I know I'm just going through the motions. Before the accident, if I had let a project slip or if I hadn't been fully present for my team, I would have eaten myself alive with guilt. I would have felt terrible, like I was letting everyone down. But now? I see the numbers, I see the lack of engagement, and it just washes over me. It's just data. 

So, no, I don't sit around feeling worthless or guilty. It's more like... I just feel entirely detached from the concepts of worth or guilt altogether. They require a level of emotional investment that I just haven't had since that day on the site. I'm just blank. It's frustrating, in a logical way, because I know who I used to be and how much I used to care about doing the right thing and being a good person, a good husband, a good boss. But the feelings that go along with that, the guilt when you fall short? They're completely gone, just like everything else.
Have you noticed that you have trouble focusing, making decisions, or thinking clearly almost every day?

No, not at all. Actually, my focus is... well, it's completely fine. The mechanics of my brain still work perfectly. As a manager, I have to make decisions all day long, and that hasn't changed. Just last week, for example, we had this massive quarterly review—spreadsheets, projections, resource allocations across three different departments. I sat in that conference room for four hours, going through it line by line. I didn't lose my place, I didn't forget what we were talking about, I didn't struggle to understand the data at all. I made the calls on budget cuts, reallocated staff... I did exactly what I'm paid to do. 

It's almost like... like a computer running a program. The processor is fine. It computes the data, it spits out the right answer. But there's no... no user behind the screen caring about the output. Does that make sense? When I have to decide whether to approve a vendor contract, I read the contract, I see the clauses, I know exactly what the liability risks are. My bachelor's is in business, I've been doing this for over twenty years, so the analytical part of my brain just clicks right into gear. I can spot an error in a fifty-page document just as fast as I could before the accident. I don't sit there staring blankly at the page trying to force my brain to work. I just read it, process it, sign it, and hand it back. 

So, no, the thinking clearly part isn't the issue. If anything, I almost wish my brain *would* fog up a little bit, just so I'd have a tangible excuse to step back, you know? Give my wife a reason to understand why I'm so disconnected, or give my team a reason to cut me some slack. But no, my thoughts are sharp. They're just... completely hollow. I make the decision, and then I just don't care what happens next. So, yeah, my focus and decision-making are completely intact. It's just the caring about the decisions that's gone.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight almost every day since the accident?

No, no changes there. My weight is... well, it's exactly what it was a year and seven months ago. I still weigh 185 pounds, give or take a pound depending on the day. I step on the scale sometimes, just out of habit, because my wife keeps it right by the shower, and it never really moves. It's funny, I guess, because you hear about people who go through... well, a major event, and they either stop eating entirely and just waste away, or they eat everything in sight trying to find some kind of comfort. But I don't do either of those things. I just eat exactly what I'm supposed to eat. 

My wife, she makes dinner every night. She's great about that, keeping the routine going. We usually have chicken, or maybe pasta, a salad. And I sit down at the dining room table at 6:30, and I eat it. I clear my plate. I don't eat it because I'm ravenous, and I don't push it away because I'm repulsed by it. I just eat it because it's on the plate and it's dinner time. It's the exact same thing with lunch at the office. I'll go down to the building's cafeteria right at 12:15, grab a turkey sandwich, and eat it at my desk while I look over those vendor contracts I was telling you about. 

I don't really care about the food, you know? I mean, my tastebuds work, I know I'm eating turkey or chicken, but there's no... there's no real satisfaction in a good meal anymore. I used to love grilling on the weekends, making these big ribeyes, marinating them all afternoon. I haven't fired up the grill since before the accident. But I still eat the required amount of calories. So, my appetite hasn't actually changed in terms of volume, and my suits still fit exactly the same. It's just another mechanical process for me now, like the focus or the physical energy we talked about. Fuel in, keep the engine running. I just chew and swallow because that's what you're supposed to do to maintain the body. So, no, no weight loss or weight gain or anything like that.
Have you had a depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years now?

Two years? No, definitely not two years. I mean, like I was saying earlier, the retrofit accident on the site was exactly a year and seven months ago. I know the exact timeline because, well, it's the dividing line of my life, isn't it? Before that day, I was completely... I was normal. I was happy, even. I remember we took a trip up the coast just a couple of months before the accident, so maybe twenty, twenty-one months ago? And I was in a great mood. I was laughing, my wife and I were walking around this little harbor town, I was fully engaged with my life. There was no depression, no sadness, none of this... this void. So the math on two years just doesn't add up at all. 

And honestly, even for the last year and seven months, I don't know if "depressed" is the right word for what I have going on. When I think of a depressed mood, I think of someone who is deeply sad, someone who is crying all the time, someone who feels heavy with sorrow or despair. I don't feel sorrow. I don't feel much of anything. I just feel... nothing. I told you about the emptiness earlier, right? It's like someone just pulled the plug and drained all the emotion out of me. I'm not sitting in my office feeling miserable or weeping over my quarterly reviews. I'm just staring at them feeling completely indifferent. 

So, no, I haven't been depressed for two years. It's only been since the accident, and even then, it's not a sad mood, it's just this absolute, persistent blankness. I just wake up, go to work, come home, eat the dinner my wife makes, and go to bed. There's no sadness, just a flat line. I think people confuse being empty with being sad, and from where I'm sitting, they are very, very different experiences. Sadness means you still care that something is wrong. I don't even have that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt almost every day, which would help differentiate between F32.2 and F33.2.
doctor.question: Have you found yourself feeling worthless or guilty about things almost every day, even when there's no clear reason for it?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about feelings of worthlessness or inappropriate guilt, which is a symptom of depression. My profile contains 'Negative_Beliefs' (S072) about trusting my own judgment, but does not specifically include generalized feelings of worthlessness or guilt without clear reason.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I mean, I don't feel guilty. Worthless? No, I wouldn't use that word either. It's... well, it goes back to what I was just saying, right? About that emptiness. To feel worthless or guilty, you have to actually feel something, don't you? You have to care enough about yourself or your actions to judge them. And I just don't. 

I mean, take my wife, for instance. She's been incredible through all of this, for the whole year and seven months since the retrofit accident. She picks up the slack, she plans things, she tries to keep the house running smoothly while I just exist in this void. And you'd think I'd feel guilty about that. A normal person would feel guilty that their spouse is carrying all the weight, right? I can intellectually recognize that I *should* feel guilty. I can look at her doing the dishes after working a full day herself and think, "I am not contributing the way a husband should." But the actual emotion of guilt? The pit in your stomach, the shame? It's just not there. 

It's the same with work. I'm the manager. I'm supposed to be leading the team. And I know I'm not doing it with the same vigor I used to. I know I'm just going through the motions. Before the accident, if I had let a project slip or if I hadn't been fully present for my team, I would have eaten myself alive with guilt. I would have felt terrible, like I was letting everyone down. But now? I see the numbers, I see the lack of engagement, and it just washes over me. It's just data. 

So, no, I don't sit around feeling worthless or guilty. It's more like... I just feel entirely detached from the concepts of worth or guilt altogether. They require a level of emotional investment that I just haven't had since that day on the site. I'm just blank. It's frustrating, in a logical way, because I know who I used to be and how much I used to care about doing the right thing and being a good person, a good husband, a good boss. But the feelings that go along with that, the guilt when you fall short? They're completely gone, just like everything else.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences a diminished ability to think or concentrate, which is relevant to distinguishing between major depressive disorder and persistent depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you noticed that you have trouble focusing, making decisions, or thinking clearly almost every day?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulties with concentration, focus, or decision-making, which is not included in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, not at all. Actually, my focus is... well, it's completely fine. The mechanics of my brain still work perfectly. As a manager, I have to make decisions all day long, and that hasn't changed. Just last week, for example, we had this massive quarterly review—spreadsheets, projections, resource allocations across three different departments. I sat in that conference room for four hours, going through it line by line. I didn't lose my place, I didn't forget what we were talking about, I didn't struggle to understand the data at all. I made the calls on budget cuts, reallocated staff... I did exactly what I'm paid to do. 

It's almost like... like a computer running a program. The processor is fine. It computes the data, it spits out the right answer. But there's no... no user behind the screen caring about the output. Does that make sense? When I have to decide whether to approve a vendor contract, I read the contract, I see the clauses, I know exactly what the liability risks are. My bachelor's is in business, I've been doing this for over twenty years, so the analytical part of my brain just clicks right into gear. I can spot an error in a fifty-page document just as fast as I could before the accident. I don't sit there staring blankly at the page trying to force my brain to work. I just read it, process it, sign it, and hand it back. 

So, no, the thinking clearly part isn't the issue. If anything, I almost wish my brain *would* fog up a little bit, just so I'd have a tangible excuse to step back, you know? Give my wife a reason to understand why I'm so disconnected, or give my team a reason to cut me some slack. But no, my thoughts are sharp. They're just... completely hollow. I make the decision, and then I just don't care what happens next. So, yeah, my focus and decision-making are completely intact. It's just the caring about the decisions that's gone.

inference.note: The patient continues to report a persistent absence of pleasure and emotional emptiness for over a year and seven months without any significant improvement, aligning with the criteria for major depressive disorder. There is no evidence of mood-congruent or incongruent psychotic features, manic or hypomanic episodes, or significant cognitive impairment suggestive of other disorders. The duration and persistence of symptoms keep both F32.2 and F33.2 as viable candidates.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had a significant change in appetite or weight nearly every day since the accident, as this is a key diagnostic criterion that may help differentiate between F32.2 and F33.2.
doctor.question: Have you noticed any significant changes in your appetite or weight almost every day since the accident?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite or weight, which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, no changes there. My weight is... well, it's exactly what it was a year and seven months ago. I still weigh 185 pounds, give or take a pound depending on the day. I step on the scale sometimes, just out of habit, because my wife keeps it right by the shower, and it never really moves. It's funny, I guess, because you hear about people who go through... well, a major event, and they either stop eating entirely and just waste away, or they eat everything in sight trying to find some kind of comfort. But I don't do either of those things. I just eat exactly what I'm supposed to eat. 

My wife, she makes dinner every night. She's great about that, keeping the routine going. We usually have chicken, or maybe pasta, a salad. And I sit down at the dining room table at 6:30, and I eat it. I clear my plate. I don't eat it because I'm ravenous, and I don't push it away because I'm repulsed by it. I just eat it because it's on the plate and it's dinner time. It's the exact same thing with lunch at the office. I'll go down to the building's cafeteria right at 12:15, grab a turkey sandwich, and eat it at my desk while I look over those vendor contracts I was telling you about. 

I don't really care about the food, you know? I mean, my tastebuds work, I know I'm eating turkey or chicken, but there's no... there's no real satisfaction in a good meal anymore. I used to love grilling on the weekends, making these big ribeyes, marinating them all afternoon. I haven't fired up the grill since before the accident. But I still eat the required amount of calories. So, my appetite hasn't actually changed in terms of volume, and my suits still fit exactly the same. It's just another mechanical process for me now, like the focus or the physical energy we talked about. Fuel in, keep the engine running. I just chew and swallow because that's what you're supposed to do to maintain the body. So, no, no weight loss or weight gain or anything like that.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a major depressive episode lasting at least two years, which would support a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) rather than major depressive disorder.
doctor.question: Have you had a depressed mood for most of the day, more days than not, for at least two years now?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about persistent depressed mood lasting for at least two years (Persistent Depressive Disorder/Dysthymia). This symptom is not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
Two years? No, definitely not two years. I mean, like I was saying earlier, the retrofit accident on the site was exactly a year and seven months ago. I know the exact timeline because, well, it's the dividing line of my life, isn't it? Before that day, I was completely... I was normal. I was happy, even. I remember we took a trip up the coast just a couple of months before the accident, so maybe twenty, twenty-one months ago? And I was in a great mood. I was laughing, my wife and I were walking around this little harbor town, I was fully engaged with my life. There was no depression, no sadness, none of this... this void. So the math on two years just doesn't add up at all. 

And honestly, even for the last year and seven months, I don't know if "depressed" is the right word for what I have going on. When I think of a depressed mood, I think of someone who is deeply sad, someone who is crying all the time, someone who feels heavy with sorrow or despair. I don't feel sorrow. I don't feel much of anything. I just feel... nothing. I told you about the emptiness earlier, right? It's like someone just pulled the plug and drained all the emotion out of me. I'm not sitting in my office feeling miserable or weeping over my quarterly reviews. I'm just staring at them feeling completely indifferent. 

So, no, I haven't been depressed for two years. It's only been since the accident, and even then, it's not a sad mood, it's just this absolute, persistent blankness. I just wake up, go to work, come home, eat the dinner my wife makes, and go to bed. There's no sadness, just a flat line. I think people confuse being empty with being sad, and from where I'm sitting, they are very, very different experiences. Sadness means you still care that something is wrong. I don't even have that.

inference.note: The patient has experienced a persistent loss of interest and pleasure (anhedonia) for over a year and seven months without significant variation or improvement, which aligns with the duration criteria for persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia) in F33.3. The absence of other core symptoms (e.g., depressed mood, fatigue, guilt, cognitive impairment, weight changes) and the presence of a sustained, flat emotional state rather than episodic depression reduces the likelihood of recurrent depressive disorder (F33.2) or a major depressive episode (F32.2 or F32.3). However, the chronicity and presence of at least two depressive symptoms (anhedonia and possibly reduced emotional reactivity) support F33.3 as the most likely diagnosis.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets criteria for persistent anhedonia, loss of interest or pleasure in nearly all activities, and duration exceeding two years (1 year and 7 months is insufficient for dysthymia, but the patient reports a continuous major depressive episode since the traumatic event). The absence of fatigue, guilt, and cognitive symptoms distinguishes this from a more severe major depressive episode (F32.3).
